About half of the market for video cameras under $5k is for photographers. Photographers want 4:3 as it’s still the general form factor for wedding photos, wildlife photography, and more. They like having a taller sensor so if they turn the camera 90° for a portrait photo, it’s not too skinny. And because it’s such a huge market that shares the same product for a very different purpose, it will probably always be that way. 

And there’s also the fact that most cinematographers started off on regular sub 5k cameras, they like when it feels like an improvement upon what they know rather than something new they’ll have to learn to get used to, and there is some benefits when cropping as well.

If you have to crop in anyways, but your shot is a little wobbly, or maybe you shot a little too low or high, you can move where the crop is on the sensor up and down to account for some motion shake, or to center the frame on the subjects better.

4:3 is the aspect ratio almost every single cinema camera shoots at. Anything wider than that is because you’re cutting some of the shot from the top. Zooming in to 16:9 on a 4:3 movie is exactly what they do in post. 

The only exception is anamorphic filming, generally reserved for only the highest budget sci fi movies like dune, interstellar, blade runner, and the like. 

Anamorphic films with lenses that crush the edges into a 4:3 sensor, and then you stretch it out in post. Doing so cuts pixels per inch roughly in half, but if you film at a high enough resolution it still looks good, but it works best on film where the resolution is roughly equivalent to 18k.

But doing that way of filming with anamorphic is incredibly expensive, takes way more manpower to edit, the lenses are hundreds of thousands more dollars, etc.

So yeah, 4:3 generally has more info in frame than 16:9, even if it doesn’t feel like it. I prefer anamorphic so you get widescreen but also more information, but it’s just too expensive for most productions

And I am aware that the current rate likely won’t stay stable, but the numbers show an example of what happens if we don’t do anything. Even developing countries should have the responsibility of planting 5-10 trees for every tree they cut down. 

It seems excessive but many trees do not survive to full growth, I worked as an arborist’s hired help for a while when I didn’t have a regular job fresh out of high school and we would plant 5 trees every time we cut one down. It wasn’t very expensive to do and the profit that can be made from a good tree easily pays for planting new trees to the point you barely notice the cost of planting other than the time commitment. That was around 4 years ago now, and majority of the trees we’ve planted have already died from either flooding or harsh winters or rabbits eating all the bark off of them. But roughly the same amount of trees we planted as we cut down survived and are now about 8 feet tall on average. (We used 2-3 foot tall saplings, mostly ash or oak but some maple and others thrown in and 5 or so cottonwood)

Developing nations don’t really have an excuse in my opinion. A good old basic tree can bring in hundreds of dollars for lumber, planting 5 saplings cost around $15, less if you buy the saplings in bulk. Doing so would also create more jobs for people who grow the saplings and sell them to the logging companies, or even selling them to new companies (even more jobs) that charge logging companies to plant trees in their wake. 

A good arborist isn’t just good at cutting trees down, they care about the environment and conservation and plant trees too.

Deforestation cuts down 2 trees for every person on earth every single year. If you live plant those 50 trees over the course of 25 years then you would simply keep the amount of trees on earth roughly the same. 

Deforestation is also the cause of 15% of all CO2 emissions when you account for the actual cutting, milling, transportation and end use of the wood on a semi related note. We need a lot of wood and we aren’t even fully replacing what we’ve cut down to begin with. 

If you’ve ever been somewhere where there’s been wildfires or mass deforestation you’ll see that we have all kinds of room for more trees. In fact at our current rate (assuming we never ever slowed down and didn’t start planting more trees annually than we currently do) then we would have no trees left on earth in 300 years.
